opener.heading: Week 5: Forest Friends 🌲
about: Azlyn prints four animal coats on Friday morning and builds the animals after lunch, then spends the rest of the week finding places for them to live. A tree up the living room wall on Saturday, a forest floor in a baking tray on Sunday, tracks across the hall on Monday, feeders outside the window on Tuesday, a cave in a cardboard box on Wednesday. Every day inherits the day before it. By Thursday she has a forest in the house and enough of it in her head to tell the whole week back to you through a lit sheet.

February arrives on Monday, and Groundhog Day lands on Tuesday the 2nd as a bonus note inside the afternoon: people in America gather round a hole to watch a woodchuck come up and check the weather. It sits an inch from Wednesday's hibernation cave, so the two can talk to each other. The cold does the rest of the work this week. Frost on the grass until the sun comes round the houses, bare branches with every old nest showing, and shadows that run long at eleven in the morning.
azlyn: Patterns she can carry on. Spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip, then finishing the row without you.
Where forest animals live. Roots, trunk, branches, top, and which animal belongs at which height.
Reading evidence. A print, a chewed leaf and a tuft of wool add up to an animal she never saw.
Waiting, and holding still on purpose. She fills four feeders on Tuesday and the birds come on Thursday; she hibernates on Wednesday while you count to twenty.
Telling the week back. Two tours, a puppet show, and a shadow fox that swells up the sheet as she walks him toward the flashlight.
you: Patterns are the beginning of algebra
Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in
Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three
Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it
Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice
Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring
shopping: One cardboard box big enough for Azlyn to sit up inside
A second box to flatten for the tree trunk
Brown paper bags, 4–6, or wrapping paper with a plain back
Old magazines or green paper, for leaves
Card scraps for ears, tails and beaks
Dark paper or a dark towel
Washable non-toxic poster paint in brown, black, white and orange
Crayons, one of them fat enough to rub on its side
Craft sticks, straws or spare pencils
A tuft of wool, for a trail clue
A baking tray, the biggest you own, or a large shallow box lid
Soil or sand, a few handfuls
Small stones and twigs from the yard
A pitcher and a spray bottle
A sponge, for the paw stamps
Sunflower seeds, mixed birdseed, oats with breadcrumbs, and raisins, a cup of each
The four feeders hung on January 17, brought back in (or 4 clean yogurt pots with a string through the base, if the wind has taken them)
A dish brush, a cloth and dish soap
A fork and a roll of paper towels
A washcloth and a shallow bowl
A flashlight, with fresh batteries and a spare set
Milk and a snack, for eating in the cave
Toy animals, in case the Forest Family does not come off
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his body for things set out to one side, passes them from hand to hand, and babbles in long strings that carry the rhythm of sentences and none of the words. He turns 8 months on Friday the 5th, the day after this week ends.

days.title: The Animal Coats
days.prepTonight: Cut six long strips from a paper bag or the back of the wrapping paper, and stand the paints, four saucers and a stack of newspaper at one end of the table.

opening.title: The Stamp Hunt
opening.need: 1 grocery bag · the recycling · the odds drawer.
steps: Hand her the bag and one job: find things that make a mark. A cork, a fork, a spool of thread, a tube end, a bottle cap.
Press each find into your palm and ask what shape it would leave. Take her guesses without fixing them.
Line the winners along the table edge in the order she wants to use them. That is the plan for 9:15.

main.title: Printing the Animal Coats
materials: Long paper strips cut from a paper bag or the back of wrapping paper, 6
Washable non-toxic poster paint in brown, black, white and orange
1 saucer or old plate for each color
Cardboard tube ends, 1 cork, 1 fork, 1 crumpled piece of paper towel
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Spread the newspaper, lay one strip in front of her the long way, and pour a thin puddle of each color into its own saucer.
Start the fawn. Two spots with the cork, a stripe dragged with the back of the fork, two spots again. Say it as you print: spot, spot, stripe. Hand her the cork on the third repeat.
Raccoon next. Wide dark and pale bands from a tube squashed flat, alternating down the strip like a ringed tail. She takes over after two.
Owl on the third strip: rings from the open end of a tube, rows of them, brown on brown.
Fox on the fourth: orange the whole length with the crumpled paper towel, then a white tip.

Hand her the last two strips with no pattern to follow. Those two are hers, printed however she likes. Lay all six flat to dry, wash hands, then walk the row and ask what comes next on the four you started.
main.tip: Print the first repeat and stop. She finishes the strip. A pattern she completed is one she can read back at you an hour later.

outside.title: The Bark Rubbing Walk
paras: Take paper and a fat crayon with the wrapper peeled off. Rub the crayon on its side over paper held flat against four different trunks. Oak comes out deep and ridged, birch close to smooth, and she feels the difference through the paper before she sees it. January bark holds the wet, so work the sheltered side of each trunk.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to hand now. Give him a wooden spoon and a folded washcloth, the second set out to his side so he has to reach across his body for it. He keeps up a running commentary at both of them while Azlyn prints. On the walk, hold his open palm flat against a trunk for a second.

second.title: Building the Forest Family
second.intro: The strips are dry by one o'clock. Wrapped round a cardboard tube and taped, each one stands up on the table by itself.
materials: Card scraps for ears, tails and beaks
steps: Lay the dry strips out and ask which animal each one is. Take her answer even when the raccoon has turned into a zebra.
Wrap the fawn strip round a tube with the pattern facing out and tape the seam on the inside. She holds, you tape.
Cut ears, a tail and a beak from the card scraps. She draws the shape, you cut on her line.
Tape the pieces where she points, including the ears you would have put somewhere else.
Stand each animal on the table as you go so the row grows in front of her.
Write every name on the base in marker. Fox is a name and so is Bibby.
Give them an address: a shelf, a windowsill, the corner of the table. They stay there all week.
second.tip: Tape the seam inside the tube where her fingers cannot find it. A seam she can pick at comes apart by Sunday, and these four have a week of work ahead.

alternatives: One strip, one tube, one animal, and stop there.
Draw faces onto plain tubes and skip the printing.
Sort the dried strips by color, then by pattern.
Line the animals up by height and photograph them.
outAgain: Grandparents, or whoever in the family is nearest, and she takes one animal to show them
A friend's house, if the Forest Family needs an audience under five
The park, back to the trees she rubbed this morning
A café with a window seat and paper for one more rubbing
A drive out to somewhere with more trees in it than houses

aroundWorld.title: Japan, Shinrin-yoku 🌲
paras: In Japan, shinrin-yoku means forest bathing, a walk with nothing to achieve. No route, no distance, no finish. You go in among the trees and use your senses: what you can hear, what you can smell, how bark feels under a hand. Japanese doctors send patients out to do it, and the walk counts as treatment.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Green tea and a rice ball, eaten under a tree with your coats on. Ten minutes of sitting and listening counts as the whole practice.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Japan's forestry ministry invented the word shinrin-yoku in 1982, and the name came before any of the science did.

days.krestonPM: Keep him off the tape and the tube ends and give him a big offcut of card instead, wider than his own mouth. At 7 months he pulls at paper with both hands and turns it over hunting for the other side. He runs a long string of sound at you while he works, so answer as though he asked you something.

insight.headline: Patterns are the beginning of algebra.
paras: Azlyn printed spot, spot, stripe, spot, spot, stripe down a paper strip this morning, and the work underneath it is what a nine-year-old does with x. A pattern is a rule that holds while the pieces change. Once she can say what comes next on the raccoon strip, she can find the rule in a row of cups, a clapped rhythm or a line of numbers, because one skill sits under all three. Researchers who track early math find pattern work predicts where a child lands later, alongside counting, and it adds something counting does not. You never have to name it. Print the first repeat, hand her the cork, and let her carry the rule to the end.

days.safety: Kreston is 7 months and everything he reaches goes in his mouth. Corks, tube ends and card scraps go up out of reach the moment you stop watching, on a shelf and not the table edge. Washable non-toxic paint only. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Tree on the Wall
days.prepTonight: Flatten a cardboard box or save two big paper bags for the trunk, and clear a stretch of wall from the baseboard up.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Tree That Fills the Wall

opening.title: Tearing the Trunk
opening.need: brown paper bags or a flattened box · masking tape · the cleared wall.
steps: Tear the paper into long ragged strips instead of cutting it. A torn edge looks like bark, and her hands can do it all.
Lay the strips end to end along the floor and stand her beside the line.
Ask where the branches should start. Tape a tab on the wall at that height and leave the pile until 9:15.

main.title: The Tree That Fills the Wall
materials: Brown paper bags, a flattened cardboard box, or the plain side of wrapping paper
Green paper, newspaper or magazine pages for leaves
The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals
steps: Tape the strips she tore this morning to the cleared wall as a trunk, floor to shoulder height, wider at the bottom. Overlap them until no wall shows.
Add branches from the shorter strips. She decides how many and where, and crooked ones stay crooked.
Tear leaves from the green paper or magazine pages and tape them along the branches in handfuls.
Draw a line along the baseboard and run roots below it. That line is the ground.
Sort the animals. Ask where each one lives: roots, trunk, branches, top. Tape a card shelf at that height and stand it there.
Write the four layers up the wall in marker: roots, trunk, branches, top. Read them out with her, bottom up.
main.tip: Build it at her height. A tree she can reach the top of is one she keeps adding to all week, and the ceiling end is yours.

outside.title: Choosing Her Tree
paras: Walk the route and let her pick one tree. She has to give a reason, and any reason counts. Put both arms round the trunk to see whether they meet, then count the big branches. Photograph her against it today.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and tracks Azlyn across a room now. Lay him on his back under the wall tree to look up at the leaves. Tape one green paper leaf at the height of his hand, off to one side so he has to reach across his body for it. He crumples it and passes it over.

second.title: The Forest Tour
second.intro: She knows where every animal on that wall lives. This afternoon she says it out loud to an audience that cannot get up and leave.
materials: Paper scraps and 1 crayon, for tickets
Your phone, to record one tour for Joseph
A chair each for the teddies, and a cushion on the floor for Kreston
steps: Set the chairs in a row facing the tree with a teddy in every one. Kreston sits at the end, propped against the cushion.
Make tickets. She scribbles on the paper scraps and hands one to every seat, Kreston included.
Give her the tube and the flashlight. The tube is her voice and the flashlight is her pointer.
Take a seat and be the audience. Who lives at the top. Why does nobody live in the roots. What happens up there when it rains.
Let her be wrong. Owls in the roots is a claim, and a claim beats a correct answer copied off you.
Record one tour start to finish with no retakes. Joseph gets it tonight.
Swap over. You give the tour, and she corrects you before you finish the first sentence.
second.tip: Ask for the tour twice with an hour in between. The second runs longer and adds something she worked out in the gap.

alternatives: A tour of one animal, thirty seconds, done.
Draw the tree on paper and label the layers together.
Hide the animals round the room and have her put each one back at its height.
Give the whole tour to Joseph on a video call.
outAgain: The botanical garden, greenhouse first if the wind is up
A garden center with an indoor plant section, the same trees in miniature
The park with the biggest trees you know, for the shapes of them bare
A churchyard or an arboretum, both good for old trunks in winter
A café near the garden and a hot chocolate on the way home
days.krestonPM: At 7 months the wet warm air of the greenhouse, the smell and the change in sound as the door shuts all land at once, and he goes still and stares. Carry him facing out and stop at three plants, his hand under yours on one big rubbery leaf. Back home he props against a cushion at the end of the row.

insight.headline: Explaining to someone else is how understanding gets locked in.
paras: Azlyn giving the tour is doing harder work than Azlyn being told. To explain the tree she has to put the parts in an order, find words for the joins, and run into the bits she does not have. Researchers call it self-explanation, and children who talk their way through a problem hold on to it longer than children who watched a demonstration. Her audience does not need to follow a word. Kreston and three teddies do the job as well as an adult, because the value sits in the telling. Ask one real question at the end and let the silence run while she hunts for the answer.

days.safety: Kreston sits on the floor against a cushion for the tour and never on a dining chair. At 7 months he goes over sideways with no warning. The leaf taped at his height and every loose end of masking tape come away the moment you stop watching, because both go straight to his mouth. The scissors stay with you, up on a shelf between cuts.

days.title: The Forest Floor
days.prepTonight: Empty the odds drawer into a bowl on the table (corks, clothespins, bottle caps, cotton balls, fabric scraps), dig out the biggest baking tray you own, and bring in a handful of small stones and six twigs from the yard before dark.

opening.title: The Odds and Ends Hunt
opening.need: the bowl of odds and ends · 1 baking tray · 1 jar lid.
steps: Tip the bowl into the middle of the table and let her go through it.
Give her three words: log, rock, leaf. Ask which things in the pile could be each. A cork can be a log, a bottle cap a rock.
Set the jar lid in the middle of the empty tray and tell her it is the pond. Nothing else goes in until 9:15.

main.title: The Forest Floor Tray
materials: 1 baking tray or a large shallow box lid
Soil, sand or torn brown paper for the ground
Corks, clothespins, bottle caps, cotton balls, fabric scraps
Small stones and twigs from the yard
steps: Spread the ground first: soil, sand, or brown paper torn small. Her hands do it. Sweep at the end.
Press the jar lid in and let her pour water from the pitcher. Refill it rather than telling her to go careful.
Lay the corks as fallen logs and the clothespins as branches. Stand the twigs up as trees, pushed in or taped to the tray edge.
Build one hollow under a cork to sleep in, and one heap of cotton balls for a nest.
Ring the pond with the small stones. Ask what is missing and put in whatever she names.
Leave one corner bare. You collect for it at 10:30 and fill it after lunch, so tell her that now.
main.tip: Give her the whole bowl, not a chosen handful. Deciding which cork is a log is the part she came for.

outside.title: What's Under the Leaves
paras: Take a paper bag and turn over the leaf litter at the bottom of a hedge. The underneath of January is wet, dark and busy: leaves gone to skeleton, a pill bug, an empty snail shell, twigs going soft. Lift one stone, look, and put it back as you found it. Fill the bag with moss, bark and four good twigs.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and everything goes to his mouth. Keep him clear of the tray and give him a bowl of his own with a wooden spoon and a folded washcloth in it. On the walk, hold one big dry leaf out for him to grab. He gets it to his mouth in under a second, so keep hold of your half.

second.title: Moving the Animals In
second.intro: The collecting bag has sat by the front door since eleven. Empty it into the bare corner of the tray, and the Forest Family moves in on top.
materials: The collecting bag from this morning
The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals
1 spray bottle, or a spoon and a cup of water, for rain
steps: Tip the bag onto newspaper beside the tray and go through it piece by piece. She decides what goes in.
Press the moss down as ground cover and lean the bark against a cork for a roof.
Bring the animals over one at a time. Each one needs somewhere to sleep and she picks the spot.
Write each name on masking tape and stick it on the tray edge below that animal.
Make it rain, one squeeze of the spray bottle or a spoonful tipped from a height. Watch where it runs and who chose a bad spot.
Move whoever got wet. Ask why the new place is drier and take her reasoning as it comes.
Lift the tray onto the table when she has finished. It comes down again tomorrow.
second.tip: Rain is the best thing here and she will ask for it eleven times. Set the number before you start, three rains, and hold the line, or the tray is soup by two.

alternatives: A shoebox lid and four things, and stop there.
Draw the forest floor on paper instead of building it.
Sort the collecting bag into two piles, alive and not alive.
Float the bark in the dishpan and see what else floats.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk with a list of five: something red, rough, round, soft, and older than her
The same hedge again with a flashlight as the light goes
A woodland path, for trees she has not met yet
The duck pond, to see what the water does in January
A warm bath with the moss and twigs on a tray beside it, if the weather has turned
days.krestonPM: He comes on the hunt in the carrier facing out with a hat over his ears. Stop three times and hold him up to touch a wall, a wet leaf, a cold gate. Name each one as his hand lands. At 7 months he answers every name with a run of sound, so leave him the gap to put it in.

insight.headline: Loose parts beat finished toys.
paras: A bowl of corks, clothespins and bottle caps puts a decision in front of Azlyn on every piece she picks up. The cork has to become a log, and she makes it one. Architects and playworkers call these loose parts: the more a material can turn into, the longer a child stays with it and the more she says. A toy fox stays a fox for as long as you own it. Her cork is a log, then a seat, then a bear, and each change is a thought she had. Keep a bowl of them where she can reach and top it up from the recycling.

days.safety: Small stones, corks and bottle caps sit at mouth height for a 7-month-old. The tray lives on the table between sessions and never on the floor while Kreston is loose in the room. Soil and leaf litter mean hands washed before the snack. Tip the pond out when she has finished.

days.title: Who Came Past in the Night
days.prepTonight: Lay the flour trail tonight in the room you can shut the door on, hide the animal at the end, and leave the paw stamps and the sieve on the table.

opening.title: The Four Feet
opening.need: paper · 1 crayon · the 2 paw stamps · one shut door.
steps: Draw four feet on one sheet: a bird's, a duck's, a grown-up's, and a paw with four toes. Draw them rough; she will still read them.
Ask whose is whose and take the wrong answers without fixing them. Then ask what each foot is good at. Gripping, swimming, walking, digging.
Press one paw stamp onto the paper dry so she meets the shape before the trail. Something came through the house in the night, and that door stays shut until 9:15.

main.title: The Track Trail
materials: All-purpose flour, 2 cups, in a sieve or a small bowl
2 paw shapes cut from a sponge or thick card
Dark paper or a dark towel for the prints to show up on
3 clues: a chewed leaf, a tuft of wool, a few crumbs
1 hidden animal from the Forest Family, or any toy animal
steps: The flour trail you laid last night waits behind the shut door. Open it and stand back. Let her look before anybody says a word.
Follow it from the start on hands and knees. Count the prints out loud and let her take over.
Stop at every clue and ask the same question: what does this tell us. A chewed leaf says it eats plants, a tuft of wool says it is furry, crumbs say it went past the trash can.
Find the animal at the end. She lifts whatever it is hiding under and says the name.
Now walk it backwards, animal to door, and ask which way it was going. This is the hard part.
Sweep up together. Keep half a cup of flour back for after lunch.
main.tip: Do not tell her who it was at the start. Guessing wrong for ten minutes and finding out at the end is the whole activity.

outside.title: Footprints in the Frost
paras: Early February holds frost on grass and car roofs until the sun comes round, and a mild morning gives you soft mud instead, which takes a print better. Walk the shaded side of the street and read what crossed it in the night: a cat's prints along a wall, bird feet in a puddle, her own boots on white grass. Send her across the lawn, then turn her round to see what she left.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and sits solid with both hands free. Put him at the far end of the trail on a blanket with a wooden spoon and let Azlyn crawl toward him. He tracks her the whole way and laughs before she arrives. Keep him off the floured floor, and out in the frost hold his bare palm on a cold car roof for one second.

second.title: Laying a Trail for Joseph
second.intro: Joseph walks in at six tonight with no idea there is anything on the floor. Azlyn spends the afternoon making sure there is.
materials: The paw stamps and the flour
Paper and crayons for arrow cards
One thing to hide at the end, chosen by her
steps: Walk the route with her first, no flour, and let her fix where it starts and ends. Follow her decision even when it goes through the kitchen twice.
She chooses what waits at the end and hides it herself, out of your sight.
Print the prints. She presses the stamp, you sieve a little flour onto the sponge between presses.
Make three arrow cards. She draws them, you tape them at Joseph's eye height rather than hers.
Add two clues of her own. Ask what each is meant to tell him and write her answer on the back.
Walk it once as a test, her leading and you playing Joseph. She will fix two things.
Turn the lights down at six and hand him the flashlight at the door.
second.tip: Write her clues down word for word. She will not remember the reasoning by Friday.

alternatives: One arrow, one hidden thing, thirty seconds of trail.
Lay the trail outside in chalk instead of flour.
Draw round everybody's shoes and match them back to feet.
Press a toy animal's feet into playdough.
outAgain: The big slide playground, and check under the swings for tracks
The neighborhood park, for the muddy path along the far end
A field walk, for the biggest frozen puddles you can find
The woods loop, looking for holes in banks and under roots
Another trail upstairs, if the wind has made outside a bad idea
days.krestonPM: He goes in the stroller with a blanket over his legs and a hat over his ears. February wind at the top of a slide is a different thing at his height, so keep him low and moving. Five minutes on the baby swing and no more. He is passing things hand to hand now, so give him two rings for the walk home.

insight.headline: Evidence and inference, a big idea learnable at three.
paras: A chewed leaf on the floor and a fox at the end of the hallway are different kinds of thing, and Azlyn spent the morning getting from one to the other. Scientists call the move inference: the leaf is what you can see, the fox is what you worked out. Three-year-olds do this better than the age suggests, as long as the evidence sits in front of them. Ask what does this tell us instead of who was it, and she has to say the middle step out loud. That middle step is the whole of science, and she will use it on you within a week.

days.safety: Flour on a hard floor is slippery in a way that puts adults down as fast as children. Sweep between rounds, keep it off tile and laminate near the stairs, and never lay a trail on a staircase. Sieve it rather than throwing it, so nobody breathes a cloud.

days.title: Feeding the Birds
days.prepTonight: Bring the four feeders in off their branches and stand them by the sink with the string, the four foods and the swimming bag.

opening.title: The Bird Menu
opening.need: paper · crayons · a saucer of seed, oats and raisins.
steps: Put the saucer in front of her and let her sort it. Seeds here, oats there, raisins in their own heap.
Ask which a bird would go for first. Write her answer as a menu, one line per item, with her drawing of the bird beside it.
Pin the menu on the window the feeders hang outside. She checks it against real birds all week.

main.title: What the Birds Take First
materials: The four feeders from January 17, brought in off their branches (or 4 clean yogurt pots and string, if the wind took them)
Warm soapy water, 1 dish brush and a cloth
4 foods, a cup of each: sunflower seeds, mixed birdseed, oats and breadcrumbs, raisins
steps: Line the four feeders up on the table and tip what is left of each into its own saucer. She puts them in order, emptiest to fullest.
She scrubs the pots in the warm soapy water and stands them on the tray. Sixteen days of birds leave a lot behind.
Fill each pot with one food and one food only. She will want to mix them, and a mixed pot answers nothing.
She draws a label for each one and you tape it on: a sunflower, a scatter of seed, a spoonful of oats, a raisin.
Re-tie the strings and pull every knot tight. A pot that swings loose in a February wind empties itself in a day.
Walk her past the menu she pinned on the window at 8:00 and ask which pot empties first. Write her answer on the menu.
main.tip: She will want raisins in every pot, because raisins are the good one. Let her put them in the pot she thinks the birds like least, and the test still works.

outside.title: Hanging the Feeders
paras: Hang all four in new places this time, well apart, where she can see them from a window and a cat cannot reach. A clothesline, a bare branch, a hook under the eaves, a fence post. She picks every spot and you lift her to the high ones. February is the hard month out there, and four foods in four spots ask a better question than four in one.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and passes things from hand to hand all day. Give him a clean yogurt pot and a wooden spoon beside the table and let him swap them over. He bangs the two together inside ten minutes. The seed, the string and the raisins stay well out of reach.

second.title: Binoculars and the Bird Chart
second.intro: Nothing will come to those feeders today. Birds take a day or two to find a feeder that has moved, so build her somewhere to sit and wait.
materials: Paper and crayons for the chart
Cushions and a blanket for the window seat
The Groundhog Day note: February 2, when a woodchuck is said to come up and check on winter
steps: Tape two tubes side by side for her pair, and two more for yours. Nothing goes round her neck: she holds hers to her eyes with both hands.
Let her color both pairs.
Build the window seat: cushions under the window, blanket over her knees, chart and pencil beside her.
Draw the chart with her. Five rows, one bird per row, a tick box at the end.
Sit and watch. Ten minutes is a long time at three, so set the deal now: watch, something else, watch again.
Tick nothing, and treat that as an answer. Ask why and write her reason at the bottom.
Tell her what today is. February 2, Groundhog Day. Ask what she thinks the woodchuck saw.
second.tip: Leave the chart on the windowsill with the pencil. She ticks it on Thursday when a chickadee turns up.

alternatives: One tube, one eye, and stop there.
Draw birds out of a book instead.
Count everything that moves outside for five minutes.
Put crumbs on the windowsill and watch the sill instead.
outAgain: Swimming
The quiet hour, if the after-school crowd is in
Indoor playground if the pool is shut
A warm café and the new binoculars, aimed at the pigeons
Straight home, if the morning ran long
days.krestonPM: He swims too if he is coming. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at it, and twenty minutes is enough before he goes cold. Hold him chest to chest for the first few minutes, so the echo and the shouting arrive with your face in front of him. Get him dry and dressed before you deal with yourself.

insight.headline: Delayed payoff is a muscle, and this is a gentle way to work it.
paras: She filled four feeders this morning and no bird came this afternoon. That gap is the thing worth having. Waiting well builds through small waits with something visible at the end, and a feeder outside the window is the friendliest version. Nobody is asking her to sit still in front of a marshmallow. She hung it, she can see it, and the birds arrive on Thursday. Say out loud that they need a day or two to find it, so the wait carries a reason instead of an unexplained no. A three-year-old who waited and turned out right takes that with her.

days.safety: Old feeders carry droppings, so both pairs of hands get washed with soap after the scrubbing and again after the hanging, before anybody eats. Loose seed on the floor is choke-sized for a 7-month-old, so sweep before Kreston goes down. The string gets tied outside and the ball comes straight back indoors, because a loop of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk. The binoculars stay stringless for the same reason: no cord long enough to go over her head, on those or on anything else in the house. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Long Sleep
days.prepTonight: Empty the biggest box in the house, check inside for staples, and stand it on its side in the corner with a folded blanket beside it.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Library Book in the Cave

opening.title: The Winter Sleepers
opening.need: the Forest Family animals or any toys · 1 blanket · the sofa.
steps: Line the animals along the arm of the sofa. Ask which of them she thinks sleeps the whole winter.
Hand her the four that do in this house's version: bear, groundhog, chipmunk, bat. Tuck them under a corner of the blanket together.
Ask what a sleeping animal needs. Take her list as it comes, and tell her the cave gets built at 9:15.

main.title: The Bear Cave
materials: 1 large cardboard box, big enough for her to sit up in
Newspaper or scrap paper to tear for leaves
The Forest Family animals, or any toy animals
steps: Lay the box on its side with the opening facing away from the window. Run a hand round the inside for staples and tape over the ones you find.
Tear the paper into leaves together. Fill a grocery bag and let the tearing run as long as she wants.
Line the floor of the cave with the leaves, the blanket over them, and the cushion at the back wall.
Tape a flap of card across part of the opening so the inside goes dark. She decides how much light gets in.
Send her in with the flashlight and stay outside. Give her five clear minutes on her own before you ask a single question.
Move the animals in one at a time, each to a spot she picks. Then get in with her, turn the flashlight off, and let the cave go dark.
main.tip: Let her tear far more paper than the cave needs. Two hands pulling in opposite directions is work she can keep up for twenty minutes.

outside.title: Empty Nests in Bare Trees
paras: Nests show up in February and vanish again in April, so this is the month to look. Walk the road and the park with your eyes up and count the dark clumps in the bare branches. Some are nests, some are a knot of twigs. Find the highest and the lowest. Nobody is home in any of them, so say so.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Sit him at the cave mouth propped on a cushion with you beside him, and let Azlyn crawl in and out past him. The light drops as she goes in and comes back as she comes out, and he turns his head after it. Give him a big sheet of paper to crush in both hands.

second.title: Waking the Bears
second.intro: The cave is dark and lined by lunchtime. Azlyn runs the afternoon on a wooden spoon and a pan lid, and winter ends whenever she says it does.
materials: 1 cup of warm milk and a snack, for eating inside
steps: Everybody hibernates. Into the cave or under a blanket, eyes shut, and hold it while you count to twenty out loud.
Bang the pan lid once with the spoon. That is spring. Everybody wakes, stretches and comes out slow.
Go round again with her holding the spoon. She decides how long winter lasts, three seconds the first time and two minutes the fourth.
Change one rule each round. Sleep standing up. Sleep in a pile. Sleep with the flashlight on. Sleep and snore.
Creep past a sleeping bear without waking it, then swap and let her creep past you. Getting caught is the fun of it, so get caught.
Take the milk and the snack into the cave and eat in there with the flashlight on.
Read the books in the cave and finish with everybody asleep and nobody banging anything.
second.tip: Let her hold the pan lid for most of the rounds. Deciding when winter ends is a lot of power for a three-year-old.

alternatives: A blanket over two sofa cushions instead of a box.
Sleeping lions, the quiet version, five minutes and done.
Draw what a bear dreams about all winter.
Sort the animals into sleepers and stay-awakes.
outAgain: The library, and ask at the desk for one book about bears and one about winter
Indoor playground if the library is shut or packed
The park on the way back, for twenty minutes of running
A café, with both new books read cover to cover
The bookshop window, if the library run is not happening today
days.krestonPM: Sit him in the board-book corner at the library while Azlyn chooses. At 7 months he mouths every book he gets hold of, and he holds one in each hand and swaps them. Let Azlyn pick his and carry it to the desk. At home the pan lid stays well away from his ears.

insight.headline: Pretending to sleep is real self-regulation practice.
paras: Azlyn lying still with her eyes shut while you count to twenty is doing something hard on purpose. She wants to move, she knows the rule, and she holds herself to it anyway. Researchers call that inhibitory control, and games with a stop-and-go rule build it better than being told to sit still, because the rule belongs to the game. The round where she holds the pan lid works harder: running the stop and the go for somebody else takes more control than following it. Freeze games, musical statues and sleeping lions sit in the same family. Reach for one on the afternoons she is climbing the walls.

days.safety: Kreston is 7 months and cannot get himself out of anywhere. He goes in the cave only with you in it, and never on his own for a second. Torn paper and loose blankets stay clear of his face. Check the box for staples before either of them climbs in, and tape over every one you find.

days.title: The Shadow Forest
days.prepTonight: Flatten two cereal boxes onto the table with the scissors and a marker, put fresh batteries in the flashlight, and clear the wall.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Puppet Show Behind the Sheet

opening.title: Guess the Shadow
opening.need: 1 flashlight · a pale wall · 3 toy animals · your hands.
steps: Turn the big light off, sit her facing the wall, and hold the flashlight behind your shoulder.
Put one animal in the beam. Ask which one it is before she turns round.
Move it closer to the flashlight and let the shadow swell. Hand her the flashlight until 9:15.

main.title: The Shadow Animals
materials: A pale wall or a white door
steps: Draw the four animals on the cereal box: fox, owl, deer, raccoon. Big simple outlines, no detail inside. You draw, she directs.
Cut them out. Card this thick is adult work: she holds the box flat while you cut.
Tape a craft stick low on the back of each, so her hand stays out of the beam.
Test the first one against the wall. If the ears are too small or the legs have joined into a block, cut wider and test again.
Do the same to all four. Deer antlers have to be fat, and an owl needs a notch between its ear tufts.
Line them up and test from across the room. Any animal she cannot name goes back for cutting.
main.tip: Cut everything fatter than looks right. Thin legs and fine antlers vanish on the wall.

outside.title: The Longest Shadow
paras: Stop at the feeders on the way out. The sunflower seeds have gone down, and a chickadee comes back for more if you hold still. Let her tick the chart when you get in. The sun stays low all day in early February, so shadows run long. Stand her on the sidewalk at eleven, draw round her shadow in chalk, and pace it out in her steps. Come back past the chalk mark on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Lay him on his back and hold the flashlight above him off to one side, your hand between the beam and his face. Move your fingers through it. He follows the shape across the ceiling, loses it, finds it again. Outside, park him with the low sun behind him and wave from a few feet back.

second.title: The Puppet Show Behind the Sheet
second.intro: A sheet clipped across a doorway turns the week into something she can perform. She has four animals, one flashlight, and an audience.
materials: A doorway, or 2 dining chairs back to back
Paper and crayons for tickets and a poster
steps: Clip the sheet across the doorway, pulled tight, floor to above her head. Two chairs back to back work if clips will not hold.
Stand the flashlight behind the sheet on the floor or a low stool, aimed at the middle.
Test the distance. Close to the sheet the fox is small and sharp; back near the flashlight he is huge and soft.
Make the poster and the tickets. She draws, you write the words she dictates.
Sit the audience down: Kreston propped on cushions, teddies either side, whoever else is home.
She tells the week back through the puppets: coats on Friday, the tree on Saturday, somebody past in the night on Monday. Give her the day and she supplies the rest.
Swap sides at the end. You run the fox, and the last five minutes go with the flashlight off.
second.tip: Move the flashlight back further than feels right. A flashlight against the sheet gives one bright spot and four tiny animals.

alternatives: Flashlight and bare hands on the wall, no sheet and no puppets.
Shadow shapes on the ceiling from under a blanket.
Draw round the puppets' shadows on paper and color them in.
Retire the puppets into the forest floor tray and stop there.
outAgain: The garden center, for the indoor trees and a warm greenhouse in February
The hardware store, for flashlights and a spare set of batteries
The park on the way back, for the low sun and the long shadows
The grocery store, and she chooses one thing for Friday breakfast
Home and the sofa, if the show ran long and nobody wants a coat on
days.krestonPM: The garden center is warm and bright, so sit him on your lap for ten minutes. Hold a big leaf out to one side, where he has to reach across himself. At 7 months that cross-body reach is new work. At the show he sits in the front row, and moving shapes on a lit sheet hold him longer than a book.

insight.headline: Shadows are confusing at three, and the confusion is worth exploring.
paras: Ask Azlyn what a shadow is made of and you get real thought in the answer and no truth in it. Three-year-olds treat a shadow as a thing that belongs to an object and travels with it, rather than as blocked light. The real version takes a couple of years of flashlight time. Every test today feeds that version: close to the sheet, back near the flashlight, one hand in the beam. Hold off on the tidy explanation. Give her the flashlight, let her run the tests, and answer the questions she asks rather than the ones she has not reached.

days.safety: Loose craft sticks and straws stay off the floor while Kreston is down. They splinter, and they fit down his throat, so count them onto the table and back off it. Card this thick is yours to cut and the scissors stay with you. Clip the sheet where it can come down without bringing anything with it, a door frame rather than a curtain pole or a shelf. Stand the flashlight on the floor instead of a stack of books, and with the room lights off keep Kreston inside arm's reach the whole time.
